extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP professionals, and biotechnology stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: A retrospective analysis of legal standards and practical guidance for assessing patent eligibility and patentability of biotechnology inventions (living organisms, processes, compositions) in the United States following Diamond v. Chakrabarty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in Diamond v. Chakrabarty held that a live, man-made microorganism is patentable subject matter under Section 101 — summarized by the phrase 'anything under the sun that is made by man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court concluded that the claimed microorganism constituted a 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter' within the meaning of the Patent Act; this decision opened the door to patent protection for a broad range of biotechnology-related inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of eligible subject matter: 'manufacture' and 'composition of matter'
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analysis asks whether the claimed invention falls within statutory categories such as a 'manufacture' or a 'composition of matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Chakrabarty the Court framed the microorganism inquiry in these terms; processes, compositions, and manufactured items (including engineered organisms) can fall within these categories and thus be §101-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-naturally occurring / 'made by man' requirement for living organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Living organisms that are non-naturally occurring or that do not occur in nature without human intervention are treated as patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex Parte Allen found claims patentable where there was 'no evidence that the claimed polyploid oysters occur naturally without the intervention of man.' The PTO explicitly stated that 'non-naturally occurring non-human multicellular living organisms, including animals, [are] patentable subject matter within the scope of 35 U.S.C. 101' (PTO Notice, Apr. 7, 1988).

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO's substantive role: determination of novelty and nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office's role is to determine novelty and nonobviousness (i.e., the substantive patentability inquiries beyond §101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that patents are limited by novelty and nonobviousness assessments (the PTO's province) and distinguishes those legal standards from moral or ethical considerations, which the authors state are not criteria for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting skill determines practical scope of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate breadth and protection afforded by biotech patents are largely a function of how well the patent claims are drafted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that 'The patents for these innovations are limited only by the skill of the individuals drafting the claims,' highlighting claim-drafting as a practical determinant of patent value and enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of methods, techniques, and processes in biotechnology
rubrics_metrics.description: Biotech methods and processes (e.g., PCR, methods for isolating/stable culture of embryonic stem cells, methods of producing engineered organisms) can be patented as processes/techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include the PCR patents (US Pat. Nos. 4,683,195; 4,683,202; 4,965,188) and James Thomson's method patent (US Pat. No. 6,200,806) — illustrating that procedural inventions in biotech have been granted patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of compositions and organisms (including transgenic animals and genetically altered crops)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions of matter such as genetically engineered organisms, transgenic animals, and modified crops have been granted patents post-Chakrabarty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the 'Harvard Mouse' (US Pat. No. 4,736,866) and patents for genetically engineered herbicide‑resistant crops (US Pat. Nos. 4,940,835 and 5,188,642); the PTO and courts have treated such compositions as within §101 when they are non-naturally occurring and otherwise satisfy patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard: need to show absence in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming living organisms, a decisional standard can require evidence that the claimed organism does not exist in nature without human intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex Parte Allen's finding turned on lack of evidence that the claimed oysters occurred naturally; this illustrates that factual showings about natural occurrence can be dispositive in securing patent eligibility for living organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variance in patenting higher life forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability of higher life forms (e.g., transgenic animals) is not uniform worldwide — different countries may reach different conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the U.S. PTO issued patents for transgenic animals, Canada (Supreme Court of Canada) ruled that the Harvard Mouse was not patentable subject matter under the Canadian Patent Act (President & Fellows of Harvard College v. Canada (Commissioner of Patents) [2002] SCC 76), demonstrating international divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of patentability and moral/ethical objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and ethical objections to biotechnological inventions are differentiated from legal patentability criteria; patents are not designed to resolve ethical questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors state that while moral/ethical concerns about manufacturing living things exist, 'patents themselves are not designed to address such issues' — patent offices focus on legal standards (novelty, nonobviousness, subject matter), leaving ethical regulation to other bodies.
